source.title: FDA grants accelerated approval to dostarlimab for locally advanced rectal cancer

sentences.sentence: The US FDA granted accelerated approval to dostarlimab (Jemperli) on 19 October 2026 for adults with certain locally advanced rectal cancers.
The US FDA granted accelerated approval to dostarlimab (Jemperli, GSK) on 19 October 2026.
It applies to adults with stage II or III locally advanced rectal cancer that is dMMR or MSI-H.
The approval rests on interim results from a phase 2 study called AZUR-1.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.
On 19 October 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted accelerated approval to dostarlimab (Jemperli, GSK).
It is approved for adults with stage II or III locally advanced rectal cancer whose tumours are mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) or microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H).
The FDA says it acted four months ahead of its goal date, and that the drug had earlier received breakthrough therapy designation.
The FDA says the approval relied on interim results from AZUR-1, a phase 2 study of Jemperli alone in patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer.
Because the approval is accelerated, the sponsor must keep following patients to confirm lasting benefit.
This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

source.title: FDA approves atezolizumab in combination with chemotherapy for Stage III mismatch repair deficient colon cancer

sentences.sentence: The US FDA approved atezolizumab (Tecentriq) with chemotherapy on 8 October 2026 as adjuvant treatment for stage III mismatch repair deficient colon cancer.
The US FDA approved atezolizumab (Tecentriq) on 8 October 2026 for stage III dMMR colon cancer.
It is given with a fluoropyrimidine and oxaliplatin as adjuvant treatment.
The approval rests on a randomised, open-label trial called ATOMIC.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.

On 8 October 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved atezolizumab (Tecentriq, Genentech) with a fluoropyrimidine and oxaliplatin for adjuvant treatment of stage III mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) colon cancer.
The approval covers adults and children aged two years and older.
A subcutaneous form, Tecentriq Hybreza, is approved with the same chemotherapy for patients aged 12 years and older who weigh at least 40 kg.
Adjuvant treatment is given after surgery to lower the chance of the cancer returning.
The FDA says the approval rests on the ATOMIC trial, a randomised, open-label, active-controlled study in people with stage III dMMR colon cancer after complete removal of the primary tumour.
This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

source.title: FDA approves tucatinib with trastuzumab and pertuzumab for the maintenance treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer

sentences.sentence: The US FDA approved tucatinib (Tukysa) on 7 October 2026 with trastuzumab and pertuzumab as maintenance treatment for advanced HER2-positive breast cancer.
The US FDA approved tucatinib (Tukysa) on 7 October 2026.
It is used with trastuzumab and pertuzumab as maintenance treatment for HER2-positive breast cancer that is unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic.
The approved use follows induction therapy with trastuzumab, pertuzumab and a taxane.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.
On 7 October 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved tucatinib (Tukysa, Seagen, a subsidiary of Pfizer) in combination with trastuzumab and pertuzumab.
It is approved as maintenance treatment for adults with unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer that has been treated with induction therapy.
The FDA describes the patients studied as having no disease progression after induction therapy with trastuzumab, pertuzumab and a taxane.
In the trial, patients received tucatinib or placebo together with trastuzumab and pertuzumab.
This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.
